lesson.title: LLMs for data systems: semantic operators with measurable quality
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: Treat each model call as a costly, fallible operator with an explicit input, output and evaluation target.
goals: Distinguish LLM-assisted database control from LLM-powered data processing.
Calculate filter/cascade costs without assuming quality is unchanged.
Evaluate semantic pipelines against human labels and reference algorithms separately.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
Study path. Recall selection and operator ordering from lessons 2–3 and 15. Start with labeled examples and cost arithmetic before trying model inference.

This original companion follows the supplied syllabus; it is not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment. Activities and timings are practice guidance. Assigned readings, assessment rules, deadlines and submission arrangements remain unverified.

sections.title: Two directions, two correctness problems
sections.html:
LLMs for a DBMS can help draft SQL, explain plans or propose configurations. The DBMS still needs to validate syntax, schema, permissions and resource use. Executable SQL can answer the wrong question: a join can duplicate rows, a time predicate can use the wrong boundary, or an aggregate can omit a group.

A data system for LLM operations organizes extraction, semantic filtering, joining, ranking or aggregation over many records. Here, outputs may vary and the operation’s meaning may be partly specified in natural language. Define what constitutes a correct extracted field or positive label, preserve evidence spans, and give uncertain outputs an explicit representation.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves context for a generator; it does not turn the generator into a transactional database. Record dataset snapshot, embedding/model version, retrieval settings and prompt version. Treat document text as data rather than instructions to change tools, reveal secrets or bypass access rules.

Key takeaway

SQL execution correctness, interpretation of the question, semantic-label quality and grounded answer quality are separate checks.

sections.title: Worked example: push a cheap filter before an expensive operator
sections.html:
Original pipeline. A public collection contains 20,000 product-support notes. The research question concerns notes from 2025 about battery overheating. A deterministic date filter retains 4,000 notes. An LLM classifier costs a hypothetical $0.002 per note, excluding all other charges. Classifying before filtering costs $40; filtering first costs $8. This saving is valid only if the date field is trustworthy and the semantic predicate does not require evidence from excluded notes.

Now add a small-model classifier costing $0.0002 per retained note, routing 25% of notes to the expensive model. Estimated classification cost is 4,000×0.0002 + 1,000×0.002 = $2.80, before calibration, retries and optimization. The expensive model may still be wrong, and the cheap model can confidently miss positives. Confidence routing is a mechanism to test, not a quality certificate.

Use a labeled calibration set to choose thresholds, then evaluate on a separate test set. Report the cost of labeling, calibration and prompt/model selection. For privacy-sensitive or licensed material, obtain permission before sending it to an external model provider; a public/synthetic dataset or approved local inference avoids that particular transmission.

Against the independent labels, a true positive (TP) is a real overheating note returned as positive; a false positive (FP) is a non-overheating note returned as positive; a false negative (FN) is an overheating note missed. Precision asks “of the returned positives, how many are right?”: TP/(TP+FP). Recall asks “of all real positives, how many did we find?”: TP/(TP+FN).

Exercise: a cascade labels 400 true positives correctly, misses 100 positives, and produces 50 false positives. Find precision and recall.

Worked answer. Precision is 400/(400+50) ≈ 0.889. Recall is 400/(400+100)=0.8. A lower call bill cannot compensate for missing a required recall target.

sections.title: Recent systems and what their guarantees mean
sections.html:
LOTUS (PVLDB 2025) introduces natural-language-parameterized semantic operators and optimized implementations. Its correctness target is statistical accuracy relative to a specified high-quality reference algorithm. A reference model can share systematic errors with an optimized model, so agreement with that reference is distinct from truth against independent human labels. Operator-level guarantees also need careful composition analysis.

DocETL (PVLDB 2025) targets complex document processing with agent-guided rewrites and plan evaluation. Decomposing data or tasks can recover information missed by a single large prompt. Its empirical evaluation concerns four document tasks, not all document workloads. Inspect the judging process, data splits and optimization cost before adopting a rewrite.

The important design space includes model choice, prompt choice, chunking, batching, selective invocation and reuse. Changing execution can also change meaning. For example, chunk-level summaries can omit a rare clause; deduplication can collapse distinct events; a join shortlist can remove the only true match.

sections.title: A complete quality and cost evaluation
sections.html:
1. Define labels: write an annotation guide with inclusion/exclusion examples, uncertain cases and evidence-span requirements. Adjudicate disagreements on a sample.
  2. Build baselines: deterministic rules where meaningful, a single-model pipeline and the proposed optimized pipeline. Keep source data and task definition fixed.
  3. Freeze evaluation: split development, calibration and test material by source document or entity to avoid near-duplicate leakage. Never optimize on the final test labels.
  4. Measure quality: precision/recall/F1 for extraction or classification, row/field-level errors, unsupported claims and important subgroups. Use blinded human checks where an LLM judge may share bias.
  5. Measure resources: calls, input/output tokens, cost under a stated price assumption, wall time, p95 latency, retry rate, peak memory and optimizer-search cost.

Store raw outputs and prompt/model versions. A deterministic seed does not guarantee bit-identical inference on every backend. Evaluate repeated runs when nondeterminism changes the outcome.

Exercise: your optimized pipeline agrees with a reference LLM on 98% of examples. May you claim 98% factual accuracy?

Worked answer. No. The reference may be wrong or biased, and both systems may make the same errors. Report reference agreement as such, then compare against an independently designed factual or human-labeled evaluation.

sections.title: H100-sized mini-experiment: semantic-filter batching and cascades
sections.html:
Trace the routing first. Use four held-out notes with independent labels positive, negative, positive, negative. Suppose the cheap model returns positive, negative, uncertain, negative; route only the third note to the expensive model. If it returns positive, the final decisions recover both positives with one expensive call. If the cheap model had confidently called that third note negative, routing would miss it entirely. This small trace explains why calibration must measure missed positives, not just confidence scores.

Inferred feasibility, not a reproduction claim. Use public or synthetic documents and a small open-weight instruction model whose license permits the experiment. A roughly 8-billion-parameter model has about 16 GB of two-byte weights; runtime memory also includes the key/value (KV) cache of attention state for processed tokens, intermediate activations, workspaces and allocator overhead. Context length, batch size, model architecture, precision and implementation determine whether a run fits. Inspect actual H100 memory and the serving engine before choosing limits.

On one H100, measure this fixed semantic-filter task under several batch sizes (notes handled together) and maximum context lengths, holding prompts, model and quality evaluation constant. Compare one-model inference with a cheap-model/expensive-model cascade using sequential loading if necessary. Reserve independent labeled data for threshold calibration and testing. Do not call a cascade superior unless its recall/precision target and end-to-end cost both hold.

An optional two-H100 extension compares independent replicas for throughput against model/tensor parallelism only when supported and meaningful. Measure host orchestration, interconnect topology and communication overhead; do not assume two devices form one freely usable memory pool. This exercise is not training a foundation model and does not promise a novel result.

Primary sources: vLLM Optimization and Tuning.

sections.title: From a prototype to a safe research claim
sections.html:
A defensible claim looks like: “On this held-out public corpus, with this label policy and model version, the cascade reaches the declared quality threshold at lower measured cost.” It names the operating point and the excluded cases.

Exercise: a prompt rewrite was chosen after inspecting all test errors, then evaluated again on the same set. How should you repair the study?

Worked answer. Treat that set as development data. Freeze the rewrite and evaluate on a new held-out set, or disclose the exploratory nature and avoid claiming an unbiased final score. Keep a record of the search budget and alternatives tried.

Key takeaway

Optimize quality, cost and latency jointly. Every shortcut needs an explicit statement of what it may change.

questions.question: What is a sound way to select a semantic-cascade threshold?
options: Choose the threshold that sends no requests to the expensive model.
Use a calibration set, then assess quality and cost on independent test data.
Tune on all final test labels and report that score.
questions.explanation: Threshold selection consumes evidence. Independent test data are needed to estimate performance after that selection.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A classifier has 400 true positives, 100 false negatives and 50 false positives. What is recall?
questions.explanation: Recall is true positives divided by all actual positives: 400/(400+100)=0.8.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Which text-to-SQL check goes beyond successful execution?
options: Confirm that the query expresses the user’s intended joins, filters and aggregation semantics.
Remove authorization checks for easier testing.
Check only whether SQL has a semicolon.
Assume every returned number is correct.
questions.explanation: Syntactically valid executable SQL can answer the wrong question. Meaning, permissions and resource use require validation.
